chapters.title: Chapter 3: Beyond VaR: Coherent Risk Measures and Backtesting

lessons.title: Expected Shortfall (Conditional VaR): Theory and Calculation

children.text: VaR answers how often a loss of a given size happens. Expected Shortfall, also called Conditional VaR or ES, answers a different and arguably more useful question: given that you are already in the bad tail, how bad is it on average? It is not a competing method to Historical Simulation, Parametric, or Monte Carlo, it is a different calculation you can run using any of the three, and it is the risk measure that fixes the subadditivity failure from the last lesson.

body.label: Expected Shortfall (ES / Conditional VaR)
body.value: The average loss across the worst (1 - confidence level) share of outcomes
body.context: Where VaR only marks the boundary of the bad tail, ES averages everything inside it.

body.caption: Informal definition for a continuous distribution: the expected loss, conditional on the loss already exceeding VaR.

children.text: This is a direct extension of the rank-based approach from Chapter 2. VaR takes the single observation at the cutoff rank. ES takes every observation from that rank outward and averages them. Consider a Rs 10,00,000 position with 100 days of historical returns, and its five worst days.

body.caption: The five worst days out of 100, sorted worst to best

body.text: ES is Rs 27,200, noticeably higher than VaR's Rs 22,000, even though both are drawn from the exact same five data points. This is not a coincidence, ES is mathematically guaranteed to be greater than or equal to VaR at the same confidence level, since it is an average across the tail rather than a single point at its edge.

children.text: Calculating ES Under a Normal Distribution

body.caption: Closed-form ES under normality, where phi is the standard normal probability density function evaluated at z-alpha. It replaces VaR's z-score with a slightly larger multiplier.
VaR vs ES for the Rs 50,00,000 Nifty position from Chapter 2 (daily volatility 1.2%)

body.text: Notice the ES-to-VaR ratio shrinks as confidence rises, 1.25x at 95% versus 1.15x at 99%. Under a normal distribution, the tail gets thinner and more tightly packed near its own boundary the further out you go, so averaging across it adds proportionally less on top of VaR. This pattern flips for genuinely fat-tailed distributions, where the deep tail can be fat enough that ES pulls further away from VaR at higher confidence, not less, which is exactly the kind of behavior the Student-t Monte Carlo example in Chapter 2 was hinting at.

children.text: Return to the two independent NCDs from the last lesson, each Rs 10,00,000, each with a 4% default probability. For lumpy, discrete outcomes like a default, calculating ES precisely requires the generalized Rockafellar-Uryasev definition, which takes the full worst (1 minus confidence) share of probability mass, splitting a single outcome's probability across the tail boundary if needed so the math works out exactly, rather than a plain conditional average.

body.caption: VaR and ES, individual bonds vs the combined portfolio, at 95% confidence

stats.label: ES of the combined portfolio
stats.context: Well below the sum of individual figures

stats.label: Subadditivity
stats.context: Rs 10,32,000 is less than Rs 16,00,000, diversification correctly looks safer

body.text: Where VaR flipped diversification logic on its head, VaR(A+B) greater than VaR(A) plus VaR(B), ES restores it correctly, ES(A+B) is well below ES(A) plus ES(B). This is not a coincidence specific to this example, Expected Shortfall is provably a coherent risk measure, it satisfies subadditivity for any distribution, not just normal or elliptical ones. This is precisely why the Basel Committee's post-2019 market risk framework requires banks to hold capital against 97.5% Expected Shortfall rather than 99% VaR.

body.title: Compute ES from the Worst Observations
body.prompt: A Rs 20,00,000 position has these four worst days out of a 40-day sample: -Rs 60,000, -Rs 54,000, -Rs 48,000, -Rs 42,000. Using the nearest-rank convention, the 90% VaR uses rank 4 of 40. What is the 90% ES, the average of all four worst days, in rupees?
body.explanation: Average of 60,000, 54,000, 48,000, and 42,000 is 204,000 divided by 4, which is Rs 51,000. Compare this to the 90% VaR of Rs 42,000, the single 4th-worst observation, ES is higher, as it always is at the same confidence level.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is Expected Shortfall described as a coherent risk measure while VaR, in general, is not?
options: ES is always a smaller number than VaR, so it is more conservative
ES satisfies subadditivity for any distribution, while VaR can violate it for skewed or discontinuous risks like default events
ES does not require any historical data to compute
ES is only used for options, while VaR is only used for equities
body.explanation: Coherence is about satisfying all four axioms, monotonicity, positive homogeneity, translation invariance, and subadditivity, for any distribution. ES satisfies subadditivity universally, which is exactly the property the bond example showed VaR failing.

body.text: VaR marks the edge of the cliff. Expected Shortfall tells you how far the drop actually is. When the shape of the risk is unusual, skewed, discontinuous, credit-like, that difference is not academic, it changes which portfolio looks safer.

points: Expected Shortfall is the average loss across the worst (1 minus confidence) share of outcomes, always greater than or equal to VaR at the same confidence level.

It can be computed from any of the three VaR methods: averaging the tail ranks in Historical Simulation, a closed-form normal-distribution formula in the Parametric method, or averaging the worst simulated outcomes in Monte Carlo.
Applied to the non-subadditive bond example from the last lesson, ES correctly shows the combined portfolio as less risky than the sum of its parts, unlike VaR.

Expected Shortfall is a coherent risk measure by construction, satisfying subadditivity for any distribution, which is why Basel's post-2019 market risk framework shifted regulatory capital from 99% VaR to 97.5% Expected Shortfall.

Knowing a model's VaR is well calibrated is not the same as knowing it is trustworthy day to day, the next lesson covers backtesting, the discipline of checking whether a VaR model's real-world breach rate matches what it promised.
